children.note: Birth in Calcutta, a devotional childhood, college and the national movement. Līlāmṛta chapters 1–2.

1 Sep 1896 · Tollygunge, Calcutta: Abhay Charan De was born the day after Janmāṣṭamī, at his mother's family home in Calcutta. His parents, Gour Mohan De and Rajani, were Vaiṣṇavas, and they named him Abhay Charan: one who is fearless under Kṛṣṇa's shelter.

He was born into a devout Vaiṣṇava household, and his name means fearless at Kṛṣṇa's feet.

Childhood (about age 6) · Harrison Road, Calcutta: Gour Mohan raised his son to love Kṛṣṇa: daily visits to the Rādhā-Govinda temple across the road, kīrtana and mṛdaṅga lessons. Abhay ran his own eight-day Ratha-yātrā with a small cart his father helped him restore, and at about six he asked for Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa Deities to worship himself.

1922 · Ultadanga, Calcutta: A friend, Naren Mullik, almost dragged a reluctant Abhay to meet a sādhu on a Calcutta rooftop. Before any small talk, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī asked these educated young men to preach Lord Caitanya's message everywhere. Abhay argued for Indian independence first, lost the argument gladly, and accepted him as his guru in his heart.

He registered the League of Devotees, a society meant to train preachers for the whole world, and opened it with a full day of kīrtana and lectures. A young doctor, Prabhakar Misra, became his first initiated disciple.

17 Sep 1959 · Keśavajī Gauḍīya Maṭh, Mathurā: After his guru appeared again in a dream asking him to take sannyāsa, his Godbrother Keśava Mahārāja insisted he accept it. In a small ceremony he received the saffron cloth and staff and the name Bhaktivedanta Swami. For him sannyāsa was the step that would take him to the West.

children.note: 1962–Jan 1965 · Delhi: His first book, Easy Journey to Other Planets, came out in 1960. Then, with a donation from Hanuman Prasad Poddar and money he begged door to door, he printed the first volume of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam in Delhi and sold it himself. Two more volumes followed, the third finished by January 1965 with help from Sumati Morarji.

children.topic: Jaladuta voyage and two heart attacks
children.note: 13 Aug – 17 Sep 1965 · Calcutta to Boston, by sea: At sixty-nine he left Calcutta on the cargo ship Jaladuta, on a free ticket arranged by Sumati Morarji. In the Red Sea he suffered two heart attacks in two days and felt he might die. After a dream in which Kṛṣṇa, rowing a boat, told him not to fear, the attacks stopped, and the Atlantic crossing was unusually calm.

Abhay Charan De was born the day after Janmāṣṭamī, at his mother's family home in Calcutta. His parents, Gour Mohan De and Rajani, were Vaiṣṇavas, and they named him Abhay Charan: one who is fearless under Kṛṣṇa's shelter.

Abhay joined Scottish Churches' College, a respected Christian college close to home. He studied English, Sanskrit, philosophy and economics, and while a student his father arranged his marriage to Radharani Datta.

After passing his final B.A. exams, Abhay would not accept the diploma, in answer to Gandhi's call to boycott British institutions. He began wearing hand-spun khādī and took a job managing a department at Dr. Kartick Bose's pharmaceutical laboratory.

children.topic: Jaladuta voyage and two heart attacks
children.note: At sixty-nine he left Calcutta on the cargo ship Jaladuta, on a free ticket arranged by Sumati Morarji. In the Red Sea he suffered two heart attacks in two days and felt he might die. After a dream in which Kṛṣṇa, rowing a boat, told him not to fear, the attacks stopped, and the Atlantic crossing was unusually calm.

The Jaladuta reached Boston on 17 September 1965 after a 35-day journey. On board he wrote a Bengali poem, “Mārkine Bhāgavata-dharma”, asking Kṛṣṇa why He had brought him to such a materialistic place and begging for the power to convince the people. He offered himself as a puppet in Kṛṣṇa’s hands.

children.topic: Lands in New York, nearly penniless
children.note: Two days later the ship docked in Brooklyn. He walked off alone, dressed as a Vṛndāvana sādhu, with forty rupees and twenty dollars from selling Bhāgavatam volumes to the captain. A Traveler’s Aid worker sent by his sponsors helped him book a return passage and catch a bus to Butler, Pennsylvania.

children.topic: A month with the Agarwals in Butler
children.note: His sponsor’s son, Gopal Agarwal, hosted him in the small town of Butler; he slept at the YMCA and cooked and spoke at the family home every evening. The local paper wrote about him, and he lectured at the Lions Club, a seminary and Slippery Rock State College. Butler showed him that Americans could understand his English and his message.

children.topic: Guest of Dr. Mishra, kept quiet
children.note: In New York he stayed first with Dr. Ramamurti Mishra, an impersonalist yoga teacher, and then in a windowless room in Mishra’s yoga studio. He was treated kindly but was rarely allowed to preach, since his praise of Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Person clashed with Mishra’s teaching. He kept translating the Bhāgavatam and led kīrtanas when invited.

children.topic: Appeals to India for help fail
children.note: He wrote to his Godbrothers, Sumati Morarji, the industrialist Padampat Singhania and the Indian government, hoping for money to buy a building for a Kṛṣṇa temple in Manhattan. Every door closed: the Gaudiya Math would not fund it, Prime Minister Shastri died, Singhania withdrew and the government refused foreign exchange. He concluded he would work without outside help.

children.topic: Driven out by a roommate’s madness
children.note: David Allen, whom he had hoped to train as his first American devotee, took LSD and went wild in the loft. Śrīla Prabhupāda walked out onto the Bowery with nothing, suddenly homeless in a foreign city. He phoned Carl Yeargens, who took him in, and he went straight on with his classes.

children.topic: His own room and first classes
children.note: He moved into a small, bare office of his own, room 307, paying the rent from book sales. Now free to preach as he liked, he held kīrtana and Bhagavad-gītā lectures three evenings a week for whoever came. He told his listeners he would rather be in Vṛndāvana but stayed in New York because his guru had ordered him to.

After a thief stole his typewriter and tape recorder from room 307, he accepted an offer to share a large artist’s loft on the Bowery, New York’s skid row, with a young man named David Allen. Musicians and artists from the Lower East Side came to chant with him three nights a week. They came for the music, but he gave them the holy name.

Michael Grant found a vacant shop with the old sign “Matchless Gifts” on Second Avenue, with a small apartment behind it, and friends shared the rent. Carrying his own suitcases, Śrīla Prabhupāda walked with them up the Bowery to his new home. The storefront became his temple and the apartment his home and study.

Howard Wheeler met the Swami on Houston Street and brought his friends to the storefront. Sitting on a mat, Śrīla Prabhupāda handed out hand cymbals, taught the beat and led the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra, and the young Lower East Side seekers chanted with him while children and passers-by gathered at the open door. He kept the door open so anyone could come in.

With the help of the lawyer Stephen Goldsmith, friends from the storefront signed as trustees of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness on 11 July 1966. He insisted on the name “Krishna” rather than a vaguer word for God. Its seven purposes, including congregational chanting, building a temple and publishing books, set out the mission he would follow for the rest of his life.

Young men began serving him personally. Keith became his cook, Howard offered to type and edit his Bhāgavatam manuscripts, and others brought flowers, fruit or notes. When Howard saw the huge bundles of manuscripts, he called it a lifetime of typing; Śrīla Prabhupāda smiled and said many lifetimes.

Invited to open a peace vigil at the United Nations, he went with his followers to chant, but the organisers asked for silence, so they chanted quietly on beads. He spoke briefly: real peace comes when people accept God as owner and friend of all. Afterwards he said that if people chant Hare Kṛṣṇa, peace will come by itself.

After a Janmāṣṭamī fast on 8 September, he initiated eleven followers the next day with a fire sacrifice in his apartment, giving each beads and a spiritual name. They promised to chant at least sixteen rounds a day. A few days later he also married two of the new disciples, Mukunda and Jānakī.

On Sundays he walked with his disciples to Tompkins Square Park on the Lower East Side and led the Hare Kṛṣṇa chant for hours under a tree. Musicians and hippies joined in, and on 10 October The New York Times reported the chanting.

His San Francisco disciples held a benefit concert at the Avalon Ballroom with the city's famous rock bands, and he led the Hare Kṛṣṇa chant before a capacity crowd. Some New York disciples thought the place unfit for him, but he went to give the chanting to thousands.

Back in New York in the last week of May, he became exhausted, and over Memorial Day weekend he collapsed. A doctor found a mild heart attack, and he was taken to Beth Israel hospital while his disciples nursed him and chanted for his recovery.

Invited by his disciple Mukunda, he flew from New York to San Francisco, where a crowd of young people met him chanting at the airport. He began a new centre in a small storefront at 518 Frederick Street.

children.topic: Lord Jagannātha comes to San Francisco
children.note: A disciple found a small carved figure of Lord Jagannātha in an import shop, and he recognised it as Kṛṣṇa. Śyāmasundara carved larger forms, and he installed Jagannātha, Balarāma and Subhadrā on Lord Caitanya's appearance day, calling the city New Jagannātha Purī.

He left America on 24 July to regain his health in India and reached Vṛndāvana on 1 August. Still weak, he began planning his return to his American students after just one day, and on Janmāṣṭamī, 28 August, he gave sannyāsa to Kīrtanānanda, his first sannyāsī disciple.

Before he left for India he asked the San Francisco devotees to hold a Ratha-yātrā like the one in Jagannātha Purī. Using his sketch, they put the deities on a decorated flatbed truck and paraded down Frederick Street; he was resting at Stinson Beach, so they brought the cart to him.

After some months in India he flew back to San Francisco, tanned and much stronger, and his disciples wept with joy. Each evening he lectured on the yoga taught in the sixth chapter of Bhagavad-gītā, talks he planned to make into a small book.

He came to a bare storefront temple at 5364 West Pico Boulevard, where the altar was two orange crates. He stayed about two months, lecturing, leading kīrtana and writing, and treated this small centre with the same care as the lonely days in New York.

He visited the small Boston centre, spoke boldly to students at MIT about the missing science of the soul, and had the devotees take him to Commonwealth Pier, where he had first landed in America in 1965. There he said that now he had disciples, the work would go on even without him.

Refused a permanent US visa in May 1968, he spent the summer in Montreal. There he trained three young married couples from San Francisco in kīrtana and sent them to open Kṛṣṇa consciousness in London.

children.topic: Writing Kṛṣṇa and Nectar of Devotion
children.note: In the new La Cienega Boulevard temple, a former church where the devotees planted 108 rosebushes at his request, he wrote two books at once: Kṛṣṇa and The Nectar of Devotion. It was the most productive writing period of his life, yet he still worried that his Bhāgavatam translations lay unpublished.

He visited the new farm community in the hills of West Virginia, walking the last two muddy miles when the car got stuck. He loved its simple life and wanted it built on Vedic ideals: plain living, cows and working the land.

While his disciples in England still had no temple, he went first to Hamburg, where young Śivānanda had opened a small storefront temple within months. Only four disciples were there, yet he came at once when they called.

He arrived in London to a press reception arranged with Apple Records and stayed at first at John Lennon's Tittenhurst estate. The devotees' “Hare Krishna Mantra” record became a hit in Europe and helped pay for the Bury Place temple, which he opened on 14 December, even holding up the falling altar pillars himself.

When a few disciples tried to push him into the background, he felt ISKCON was under threat. Before leaving America he dictated a document creating a Governing Body Commission, so the society's 34 centres could be managed even after he was gone.

On a world tour in spring 1972, after laying foundations in Māyāpur, Vṛndāvana and Bombay, he flew to Mexico City. No devotees were at the airport, so he sat on his suitcase chanting until a Mexican couple who knew the devotees found him.

From Bombay he set out on 25 January on a tour of twelve major cities in fifty days, circling the globe eastward and going as far south as Venezuela. He had to be back in March for the festival at Māyāpur, where about a thousand devotees were coming.

On a tour of North American temples he came to Philadelphia for its Ratha-yātrā festival. He bowed down on the street before Lord Jagannātha’s cart, rode it through the city, and spoke to the crowd about chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. It was the biggest crowd the city’s festival had ever drawn.

He asked his Bhaktivedanta Book Trust to produce seventeen volumes in just two months, mostly Caitanya-caritāmṛta. The Press devotees worked day and night and finished on schedule, and the books reached him in Vṛndāvana around his birthday. He wrote that his own spiritual master would be pleased with their work.

Shown a grand mansion built by a car-industry millionaire, he told the owner, “We are beggars,” and asked for it as a gift. When the owner refused, he offered $300,000 cash without having a penny. Two disciples gave the money, and he left Detroit taking nothing for himself.

Back at the new Krishna-Balaram Mandir, he checked every detail: cleanliness, cooking, worship and money. He judged the whole temple by whether the bell was rung on time, every hour and half hour, even through the night. His sharp reprimands were meant to train his disciples and make the temple solid.

A telegram called him back from Canada to meet India’s prime minister. Under heavy security he met Mrs. Gandhi alone. She was anxious and the talk was short, but she agreed to his main request: permanent visas for his foreign disciples in India.

During a tour of Mauritius and South Africa, his car hit another head-on on a country road. Both cars were wrecked; he was bruised and cut but sat calm and silent. He said Kṛṣṇa had saved them, then went on to Nairobi rather than disappoint the devotees there.

Hearing of slow work and stolen materials at Hare Krishna Land, he hurried back to Bombay. He fired the engineer and hired one of India’s biggest building firms. Money from book sales in America paid for it, which he called cooperation between the lame man and the blind man.

At the 1976 Māyāpur festival, renunciants and married devotees were quarrelling over who was more qualified to lead. He told the leaders not to judge by dress or āśrama but by real advancement in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Party politics, he warned, would finish the movement.

Wanting time to write, he went to Hawaii and his translating jumped to two or three hundred digits a day on his dictating machine. He wrote to his G.B.C. leaders asking them to take over management so he could finish Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, which he called his greatest contribution.

Ten years after arriving alone and penniless, he returned to New York, where ISKCON now had a twelve-storey building. He rode the cart of Subhadrā down Fifth Avenue with about six hundred disciples chanting. As he left, he asked only for the blessing to keep fighting for Kṛṣṇa, like Arjuna.

children.topic: “A bona fide religion”: New York court
children.note: In 1977 the movement faced fierce opposition in the West, including the kidnapping and “deprogramming” of devotees. A New York judge threw out charges against ISKCON leaders and called the Hare Krishna movement a bona fide religion. Hearing it in Māyāpur, he said his mission was now successful.

Very ill after a stay in Hrsikesha, he returned to Vṛndāvana, saying that if anything went wrong he would at least be there. He called his G.B.C. leaders and made a will naming the G.B.C. as ISKCON’s final managing authority, with trustees for each property. He told them their love for him would be shown by their cooperation.

children.topic: Last visit to the West: London
children.note: Though extremely weak, he flew to London rather than stay in bed, arriving after a twenty-hour journey. At Bhaktivedanta Manor he wept with joy at the kīrtanas and at reports that book distribution in Europe had passed America. When his health worsened he returned to Bombay on 14 September.

children.topic: His disciples beg him to stay
children.note: Back in Vṛndāvana he stopped eating and spoke of dying peacefully. He asked his Godbrothers to forgive any offences and told his disciples not to fight among themselves, as he had given direction in his books. When the G.B.C. tearfully begged him to stay, he said “All right” and drank a glass of juice.

At 7:30 in the evening, in his room at the Krishna-Balaram Mandir, he left this world while devotees chanted Hare Kṛṣṇa around him. He left behind his books, his temples, his society, and thousands of disciples. His followers learned to serve him through his instructions, which they called service in separation.

Gour Mohan raised his son to love Kṛṣṇa: daily visits to the Rādhā-Govinda temple across the road, kīrtana and mṛdaṅga lessons. Abhay ran his own eight-day Ratha-yātrā with a small cart his father helped him restore, and at about six he asked for Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa Deities to worship himself.

A friend, Naren Mullik, almost dragged a reluctant Abhay to meet a sādhu on a Calcutta rooftop. Before any small talk, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī asked these educated young men to preach Lord Caitanya's message everywhere. Abhay argued for Indian independence first, lost the argument gladly, and accepted him as his guru in his heart.

A month after hearing his guru speak for hours at Kosi near Vṛndāvana, Abhay was introduced for initiation in Allahabad. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta said he had marked this young man because he liked to hear, and gave him both initiations at once. He became Abhay Charanaravinda.

children.topic: "If you ever get money, print books"
children.note: Earlier that year his English poem for his guru's birthday was printed in The Harmonist, and his guru said to publish whatever he wrote. Walking alone with Abhay by Rādhā-kuṇḍa, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta grieved over quarrels for rooms in the Calcutta temple and told him that printing books would be better.

Abhay wrote asking how a householder could serve. Two weeks before he passed away, his guru replied that Abhay could become a very good preacher in English. Abhay saw it as the same order he had heard in 1922. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta departed on 1 January 1937.

At Bhaktivedanta Manor he wept with joy at the kīrtanas and at reports that book distribution in Europe had passed America. When his health worsened he returned to Bombay on 14 September.
City of a yearly Ratha-yātrā that he attended in 1975.

On a tour of North American temples he came to Philadelphia for its Ratha-yātrā festival. He bowed down on the street before Lord Jagannātha’s cart, rode it through the city, and spoke to the crowd about chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa. It was the biggest crowd the city’s festival had ever drawn.
Where ISKCON bought the Fisher mansion in 1975.

Shown a grand mansion built by a car-industry millionaire, he told the owner, “We are beggars,” and asked for it as a gift. When the owner refused, he offered $300,000 cash without having a penny. Two disciples gave the money, and he left Detroit taking nothing for himself.
Works in this course, each with the passages where they appear.
The magazine he began in India and continued in the West.

With the Gauḍīya Maṭh split by lawsuits and Calcutta at war, Abhay wrote, edited and typed a magazine by himself in his front room. After the government refused paper because of wartime shortages, he persisted and printed Back to Godhead, under his guru's order.

children.topic: Alone in Delhi with his magazine
children.note: Homeless after leaving his Godbrothers' āśrama, he revived Back to Godhead in Delhi and did everything himself. He walked to the printer without breakfast, sold copies at tea stalls, was knocked down by a cow and collapsed from heatstroke. To India's president he wrote that he was crying alone in the wilderness.
His life’s main translation work.

His first book, Easy Journey to Other Planets, came out in 1960. Then, with a donation from Hanuman Prasad Poddar and money he begged door to door, he printed the first volume of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam in Delhi and sold it himself. Two more volumes followed, the third finished by January 1965 with help from Sumati Morarji.

After some years based in Vṛndāvana, he moved into two rooms at the Rādhā-Dāmodara temple, home of Jīva Gosvāmī and the samādhi of Rūpa Gosvāmī. Rising at 1 a.m., he translated Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, feeling the past ācāryas were sending him West.

children.topic: Sails for America on the Jaladuta
children.note: With a sponsor letter from Gopal Agarwal in Pennsylvania and a ticket from Sumati Morarji of Scindia Steamship, he finally left India at sixty-nine. He carried a suitcase, an umbrella, dry cereal and trunks of his Bhāgavatam volumes, but almost no money.

children.topic: Lands in New York, nearly penniless
children.note: Two days later the ship docked in Brooklyn. He walked off alone, dressed as a Vṛndāvana sādhu, with forty rupees and twenty dollars from selling Bhāgavatam volumes to the captain. A Traveler’s Aid worker sent by his sponsors helped him book a return passage and catch a bus to Butler, Pennsylvania.

children.topic: Guest of Dr. Mishra, kept quiet
children.note: In New York he stayed first with Dr. Ramamurti Mishra, an impersonalist yoga teacher, and then in a windowless room in Mishra’s yoga studio. He was treated kindly but was rarely allowed to preach, since his praise of Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Person clashed with Mishra’s teaching. He kept translating the Bhāgavatam and led kīrtanas when invited.

Young men began serving him personally. Keith became his cook, Howard offered to type and edit his Bhāgavatam manuscripts, and others brought flowers, fruit or notes. When Howard saw the huge bundles of manuscripts, he called it a lifetime of typing; Śrīla Prabhupāda smiled and said many lifetimes.

children.topic: Writing Kṛṣṇa and Nectar of Devotion
children.note: In the new La Cienega Boulevard temple, a former church where the devotees planted 108 rosebushes at his request, he wrote two books at once: Kṛṣṇa and The Nectar of Devotion. It was the most productive writing period of his life, yet he still worried that his Bhāgavatam translations lay unpublished.

Wanting time to write, he went to Hawaii and his translating jumped to two or three hundred digits a day on his dictating machine. He wrote to his G.B.C. leaders asking them to take over management so he could finish Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, which he called his greatest contribution.
His Gītā translation and commentary, begun as Geetopanishad in 1939.

Abhay's large factory in Lucknow had to close and he lost everything. The only copy of his Gītā commentary, Geetopanishad, was stolen from his home. He came to see a Bhāgavatam verse in his losses: Kṛṣṇa slowly takes away the wealth of those He favours.

children.topic: Preface to Bhagavad-gītā As It Is
children.note: Macmillan had agreed to print his full, unabridged Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, and in Sydney he wrote its Preface. In it he gave all credit to Kṛṣṇa and to his spiritual master, saying his only qualification was presenting the Gītā without change.
The book he lectured from in his first New York classes; later his Bhagavad-gītā As It Is.

children.topic: His own room and first classes
children.note: He moved into a small, bare office of his own, room 307, paying the rent from book sales. Now free to preach as he liked, he held kīrtana and Bhagavad-gītā lectures three evenings a week for whoever came. He told his listeners he would rather be in Vṛndāvana but stayed in New York because his guru had ordered him to.

Howard Wheeler met the Swami on Houston Street and brought his friends to the storefront. Sitting on a mat, Śrīla Prabhupāda handed out hand cymbals, taught the beat and led the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra, and the young Lower East Side seekers chanted with him while children and passers-by gathered at the open door. He kept the door open so anyone could come in.

children.topic: Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead
children.note: His summary of the Tenth Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, first printed in 1970.

At the San Francisco Ratha-yātrā the first copies of his new book Kṛṣṇa arrived, and he sold every one to the crowd himself, keeping none. It marked the start of a huge wave of book distribution by his disciples in the years that followed.
Life and teachings of Śrī Caitanya; his translation was printed in seventeen volumes in 1975.

He asked his Bhaktivedanta Book Trust to produce seventeen volumes in just two months, mostly Caitanya-caritāmṛta. The Press devotees worked day and night and finished on schedule, and the books reached him in Vṛndāvana around his birthday. He wrote that his own spiritual master would be pleased with their work.
